blocks.text: The six **cardinal respiratory symptoms** are cough, sputum, haemoptysis, breathlessness, wheeze and chest pain. **Cough** is the commonest. It is triggered when sensory nerve endings in the mucosa of the pharynx, larynx, trachea and bronchi are stimulated, and the reflex becomes over-sensitive to changes in air temperature and irritants such as tobacco smoke or perfume.

blocks.title: Cough pattern as a diagnostic clue
rows: Usually dry, **worse at night**; may be the only symptom (cough-variant asthma), also on waking and after exercise
Dry or productive, **worse in the mornings**
Productive; **change of posture** brings up sputum
Often nocturnal, may bring up **pink frothy** sputum
Raw retrosternal soreness with the cough

blocks.title: Acute vs chronic cough
items: **Acute, self-limiting:** viral lower respiratory infection, post-nasal drip (rhinitis or sinusitis), inhaled foreign body, laryngitis or pharyngitis.

**Chronic cough with normal examination, CXR and spirometry:** the big three are **cough-variant asthma, post-nasal drip and GORD**. KC Essentials says these explain about 99% of cases in non-smokers who are not on an ACE inhibitor and have a normal CXR.
**ACE inhibitors** cause a dry chronic cough in about 10–15% of users, more often women.
**Pertussis** in adults can leave a cough for up to 3 months.

blocks.title: Red flags in the cough history
items: A smoker's cough that **changes or worsens** is the commonest presenting symptom of lung cancer and must be investigated.

A cough that has lost its **explosive** quality suggests respiratory muscle weakness or vocal cord palsy. One paralysed cord gives a long, low-pitched, ineffective **'bovine' cough** with hoarseness, classically from a lung cancer invading the **left recurrent laryngeal nerve**.

**Stridor** (a noisy inspiration) means partial obstruction of a large airway, e.g. laryngeal oedema, tracheal tumour, external compression or an inhaled foreign body. It needs **urgent** investigation.

blocks.title: Sputum appearance
rows: Clear/white (mucoid), may have black carbon specks
Smoking, the commonest cause of excess mucus
Bronchial or pneumonic infection, but also eosinophils in asthma
Large daily volumes of purulent sputum

blocks.text: In an adult, especially a smoker, with a **new unexplained cough**, Davidson advises bronchoscopy or thoracic CT **even if the CXR is normal**, because a small endobronchial tumour or an unexpected foreign body can be missed on plain film.
**Yellow or green sputum does not prove infection.** The colour comes from cells (neutrophils _or_ eosinophils), so eosinophil-rich sputum in asthma looks just the same.

**Dyspnoea** is an unpleasant awareness of the need to breathe. Lung disease drives it in three ways: by stimulating **intrapulmonary sensory nerves** (pneumothorax, interstitial inflammation, PE), by increasing the **mechanical load** on the respiratory muscles (airflow obstruction, fibrosis), and through **chemoreceptor** stimulation by hypoxia, hypercapnia or acidosis. The patient feels roughly the sum of these drives.

blocks.title: Acute vs chronic breathlessness: common causes
rows: Acute pulmonary oedema, acute severe asthma, COPD exacerbation, pneumothorax, pneumonia, PE; also inhaled foreign body, laryngeal oedema/anaphylaxis, metabolic acidosis, psychogenic hyperventilation
COPD, chronic asthma, chronic heart failure, ILD, lung cancer, large effusions, chronic thromboembolism, severe anaemia, obesity, deconditioning

blocks.title: History clues to the cause of chronic breathlessness
rows: Breathless mainly on walking, little at rest or overnight; slow decline over years
Woken at night with tightness and wheeze; variation within and between days
Relentless, progressive, present even at rest, with dry cough
CO2 retention and respiratory failure (e.g. kyphoscoliosis, muscular dystrophy)
Recurrent pleuritic pain at different sites
'Can't get a deep breath in', sighing, perioral/finger tingling; rarely wakes from sleep, may ease with exercise

blocks.title: MRC dyspnoea scale
rows: Breathless when hurrying or walking up a slight hill
Slower than people of the same age on level ground, or has to pause at their own walking pace
Has to halt for breath after roughly **100 m** (or a few minutes) on level ground
Too breathless to leave the house, or breathless dressing/undressing

blocks.title: Psychogenic hyperventilation (Davidson Box 17.7)
items: Inability to take a satisfying deep breath; frequent sighing; erratic breathing at rest.
Digital and/or perioral paraesthesiae; carpopedal spasm from acute respiratory alkalosis.
**Nijmegen questionnaire score over 26**; resting end-tidal CO2 **below 4.5%**.
ABG: **normal PaO2, low PaCO2, alkalosis**.
A diagnosis of exclusion: **thromboembolism must be ruled out first**.

blocks.title: Wheeze, stridor and investigation
items: **Wheeze** means airflow limitation of any cause: generalised (asthma, COPD) or localised (tumour, foreign body), and also vocal cord dysfunction and bronchiolitis. It is not diagnostic of asthma, and may be absent early in asthma.
**Stridor** is a harsh _inspiratory_ noise from obstruction of the trachea or a main bronchus. Do not call it wheeze.
**Acute breathlessness work-up:** CXR, pulse oximetry ± ABG; ECG, FBC, electrolytes, glucose, troponin or D-dimer as indicated.
**Chronic breathlessness work-up:** simple lung function, oximetry, FBC and CXR; echocardiogram if a cardiac cause is suspected.

blocks.note: Look at: the stimuli that converge on the medullary respiratory neurons (carotid body, central chemoreceptors, vagal lung afferents, mechanical load, deflation).

blocks.text: Davidson's acute-breathlessness discriminators: **massive PE** gives central cyanosis, raised JVP, _clear lungs_ and shock; **COPD with type II failure** gives a flapping tremor and bounding pulses; **metabolic acidosis** gives deep breathing with no heart or lung signs; **psychogenic** breathlessness gives carpopedal spasm with no cyanosis.

**Orthopnoea does not separate heart from lung disease.** In COPD, lying flat lets the abdominal contents push the diaphragm up and worsens obstruction, so many COPD patients sleep propped up. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea points more to left heart failure.

**Haemoptysis is serious until proven otherwise.** First confirm the blood is coughed up and is not haematemesis or bleeding from the nose or gums. Many episodes stay unexplained after full work-up and are put down to simple bronchial infection, but this is a diagnosis made only after investigation.

blocks.title: Clues to the cause of haemoptysis
rows: Repeated small bleeds or blood-streaked sputum in a smoker
Blood mixed with large volumes of purulent sputum; childhood pneumonia or old TB
Bronchiectasis (can bleed catastrophically, as can mycetoma)
Pleuritic pain, leg swelling, risk factors
Mild bleed during a COPD exacerbation
Acute infection, the commonest cause of mild haemoptysis

blocks.title: Investigation sequence (non-massive bleed)
items: **CXR** in every patient: tumour, pneumonia, mycetoma, TB.
**FBC and clotting screen.**
**Bronchoscopy** once acute bleeding has settled: finds a central cancer not seen on CXR and allows biopsy.
**CTPA**: thromboembolism, AV malformation, small or hidden tumours.
Pocket Medicine adds sputum for bacteria, fungi, AFB and cytology, and ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA and urinalysis if vasculitis is possible.

blocks.title: Massive haemoptysis
items: Usually from **bronchiectasis or TB**, also lung abscess and late lung cancer.
**Patients die from asphyxiation, not from blood loss.** Protect gas exchange first.
Sit upright, or lie **bleeding side down** if the side is known; give high-flow oxygen; large-bore IV access; FBC, clotting, U&E, ABG, CXR; reverse any coagulopathy.
Tranexamic acid or terlipressin may limit bleeding, though evidence is limited.
A divided (double-lumen) endotracheal tube can protect the good lung. **Bronchial artery embolisation** or emergency surgery can be life-saving.
Refer early to a respiratory physician and thoracic surgeon. Cough suppressants may increase the risk of asphyxia.

blocks.note: Look at: catheter in a dilated right bronchial artery in post-TB bronchiectasis with massive haemoptysis, treated by embolisation.

blocks.title: Respiratory chest pain
rows: Sharp, localised, worse on deep breath or cough (pleuritic)
Pleural irritation, most often infection or PE
Malignant invasion of the chest wall
Anterior pain with a tender costochondral junction

blocks.text: **Examine the abdomen in every patient with pleuritic chest pain.** A liver abscess, cholecystitis, cholangitis or pancreatitis can mimic pneumonia with fever, pleuritic pain and a small (usually right-sided) effusion.

**Massive haemoptysis has no single definition.** Kumar & Clark and KC Essentials use **>200 mL in 24 h**; Pocket Medicine uses **>100 mL/h or >500 mL/24 h**. Davidson gives no volume and defines severity clinically. For our exams, quote the >200 mL/24 h figure and stress that asphyxia is what kills.
A **normal CXR does not exclude serious disease** in haemoptysis. However, when the CXR is normal, CT and bronchoscopy find a cause in only about **5%** of patients.

sections.title: General examination: hands, face, clubbing and cyanosis

blocks.text: Davidson's examination order: **hands → radial pulse → JVP → face, mouth and eyes → trachea and cricosternal distance → apex → expansion → percussion → auscultation (breath sounds, added sounds, vocal resonance) → cervical nodes from behind → leg oedema.** Start with the end of the bed: respiratory rate, cachexia, fever, accessory muscles, oxygen, nebulisers, inhalers and the sputum pot.

blocks.title: Hands, face and neck
rows: Suppurative lung disease, lung cancer, fibrosis (see below)
Flapping tremor, warm well-perfused palms, bounding pulse
Distended chest wall veins, face/arm swelling
Cor pulmonale / salt and water retention

blocks.text: **Finger clubbing** is painless soft-tissue swelling of the terminal phalanx. The nail becomes more curved in both directions, the normal angle between nail and nail fold is lost, and the depth of the finger at the nail base becomes **greater than at the DIP joint**. It is usually symmetrical and often involves the toes. Clubbing can regress when the cause resolves, e.g. after lung transplant for cystic fibrosis.

blocks.title: Causes of clubbing (Davidson Box 17.8)
rows: Suppurative: bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema, cystic fibrosis, TB. Tumours: lung cancer, mesothelioma. Pulmonary fibrosis (about two-thirds of IPF)
Cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis, AV shunts/aneurysms
Cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease

blocks.note: Look at: anterior and lateral views of clubbing, with loss of the nail-fold angle and increased nail curvature.
Look at: a clubbed finger beside a normal finger; compare the nail-bed angle.

blocks.text: Over **90%** of clubbing signals a serious underlying disorder, most often suppurative or malignant lung disease. A new finding of clubbing should prompt a CXR.
**Uncomplicated COPD does not cause clubbing**, and it rarely causes haemoptysis or chest pain. Clubbing in a COPD patient means looking for **lung cancer**, bronchiectasis or fibrosis.

**Central vs peripheral cyanosis:** central cyanosis is seen on the tongue (especially underneath) and lips, and is always accompanied by peripheral cyanosis. Peripheral cyanosis alone, with cold extremities, reflects poor peripheral circulation and not hypoxaemia.

sections.title: Chest examination: palpation, percussion, auscultation and sign patterns

blocks.title: Palpation and percussion
items: **Trachea and apex**: displaced by volume loss (pulled towards) or by fluid or air under tension (pushed away).
**Cricosternal distance**: normally **3–4 finger-breadths** in full expiration; reduced in severe airflow limitation (hyperinflation).
**Expansion**: reduced on the side of the lesion.
**Percussion**: dull (consolidation, collapse, fibrosis), **stony dull** (effusion), hyper-resonant (pneumothorax). Liver and cardiac dullness disappear in hyperinflation.
**Tactile vocal fremitus** duplicates vocal resonance and Kumar says it is not routinely needed.

blocks.title: Auscultation
items: **Vesicular** breath sounds: healthy lung filters out the high frequencies of laryngeal turbulence.
**Bronchial breathing**: consolidated or collapsed lung with a _patent_ bronchus transmits the high frequencies. It comes with **increased vocal resonance** and **whispering pectoriloquy**.
**Wheeze**: usually expiratory. **Monophonic** means a single large-airway obstruction; **polyphonic** means many narrowed small airways.
**Silent chest** in acute severe asthma: too little airflow to make any wheeze, a life-threatening sign.
**Crackles**: _early_ inspiratory in diffuse airflow limitation; _late_ inspiratory in pulmonary oedema, fibrosis and bronchiectasis. Fine 'velcro' basal crackles are typical of ILD.
**Pleural rub**: a localised creak, likened to footsteps in fresh snow, from inflamed pleura (infection, infarction).

blocks.title: Physical signs of common lesions
rows: Normal; cardiac and liver dullness lost if hyperinflated

blocks.title: Whole-patient patterns (Davidson)
items: **COPD:** pursed lips, accessory muscles, barrel chest, reduced cricosternal distance, indrawing of lower ribs on inspiration (low flat diaphragm), impalpable apex, heart sounds loudest in the epigastrium, prolonged expiration with wheeze; ± raised JVP and oedema (cor pulmonale).

**Pulmonary fibrosis:** small lungs, reduced expansion, dull bases (high diaphragm), central cyanosis, tachypnoea, fine bibasal inspiratory crackles; clubbing common in IPF; loud P2 and oedema if cor pulmonale.
**Right upper lobe collapse:** trachea pulled **to the same side**, reduced upper-zone volume and expansion, dull upper zone, reduced breath sounds with a central obstruction.

blocks.title: Bedside extras and first-look CXR
items: Check the observation chart (SpO2 and inspired oxygen), look in the sputum pot, and measure **peak flow or spirometry**. This tells you more about airflow limitation than any physical sign.
Pulse oximetry normal range is 94–98%, but it **does not measure CO2**, so take an ABG if hypoventilation is possible.
**PA film** is standard. On an **AP film** the heart looks bigger and the scapulae overlie the lungs, so do not diagnose cardiomegaly from it.
Right hemidiaphragm usually sits 2–3 cm higher than the left; cardiothoracic ratio normally <50% on a PA film; mediastinum is wide if >6 cm (upright) or >25% of thoracic width at the aortic knob.
An effusion must exceed about **500 mL** before it does more than blunt the costophrenic angle. Larger ones form a meniscus rising into the axilla.

blocks.note: Look at: left upper lobe collapse, with opacified left upper/mid zone, volume loss and trachea and heart pulled to the left.
Look at: a large pleural effusion, a dense homogeneous shadow with a meniscus on an erect film.

blocks.text: **Tracheal deviation in pneumothorax.** Davidson shows no tracheal shift in a simple pneumothorax, while **tension pneumothorax pushes the trachea to the opposite side** with tachycardia and hypotension (Kumar: large pneumothorax shifts the mediastinum away). Step-Up lists a shift _towards_ the pneumothorax; follow Davidson. Tension is decompressed at once (large-bore cannula, 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line) without waiting for a CXR.

**Volume loss pulls; fluid and air push.** Collapse and fibrosis pull the trachea _towards_ the lesion. A massive effusion or tension pneumothorax pushes it _away_. Consolidation alone causes **no** shift, so shift with apparent pneumonia suggests an obstructing endobronchial lesion.

sections.title: Health education: smoking, cessation, vaccination and prevention

blocks.text: **Smoking** is one of the top three risk factors for the global burden of disease. It causes most COPD and lung cancer, and most smokers die of these or of ischaemic heart disease. Tobacco smoke contains over 40 carcinogens.

blocks.title: Harms of smoking
items: **Cancers:** lung, larynx and upper aerodigestive tract, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, bladder, kidney, cervix.
**Vascular:** IHD, stroke, peripheral vascular disease. Also peptic ulcer.
**Maternal smoking:** fetal growth retardation, low birth weight, higher fetal/neonatal mortality.
**Passive smoking:** more frequent and severe childhood asthma, infant pneumonia and bronchitis, worse symptoms in COPD and asthma, a small rise in lung cancer risk.
**Dose and synergy:** 20 a day for 20 years raises lifetime lung cancer risk about **10-fold**; smoking plus **asbestos** raises it about **90-fold** over unexposed non-smokers.

blocks.title: Stopping smoking
rows: Health warnings, higher tobacco tax, advertising bans, smoke-free public places/workplaces
Cessation clinic, self-help, group counselling. Cost-effective
**NRT** (gum, lozenge, patch, nasal spray), **bupropion**, **varenicline** (α4β2 nicotinic receptor **partial agonist**, about doubles quit rates)
Prescribe only with a committed **target stop date**; first supply runs 2 weeks beyond it; NRT preferred, no gain from combining NRT and bupropion; switch if not abstinent by 3 months
May help quitting; long-term safety unknown

blocks.text: **Quitting slows the rate of FEV1 decline back to that of a non-smoker** (Fletcher–Peto curve). Lung function may improve a little, but the damage is not fully reversed, so the earlier someone stops, the more function they keep. Stopping smoking is the only intervention that changes the natural history of COPD.

blocks.note: Look at: FEV1 against age in susceptible smokers, and how the curve flattens after stopping at 45 vs 65.

blocks.title: Other prevention and education
items: **Vaccination in COPD:** annual influenza vaccine, plus pneumococcal vaccine as appropriate. Influenza vaccine is remade from current strains each year, protects about 70% and lasts about a year; it is given to those over 65 and younger high-risk people.
**Pulmonary rehabilitation:** exercise training, education and nutrition, usually 2–3 sessions/week for 6–12 weeks. It improves symptoms, exercise tolerance and confidence.
Also address obesity, poor nutrition, depression and social isolation.

**Air pollution:** outdoor (sulphur and nitrogen oxides, particulates) raises respiratory and cardiovascular deaths in the vulnerable. **Indoor biomass-fuel smoke** from cooking and heating is a major cause of respiratory disease in developing countries.
**Lung cancer screening (Pocket):** annual low-dose CT at age 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years, current or quit within 15 years. It cuts lung cancer mortality by about 20%.
**TB contacts:** screen with CXR and Mantoux (positive ≥10 mm at 72 h) or IGRA; BCG for high-risk groups.

blocks.title: Long-term oxygen therapy (Davidson Box 17.27)
items: Two ABGs at least **3 weeks apart** while stable on optimal treatment.
PaO2 **<7.3 kPa**; or **7.3–8 kPa** with pulmonary hypertension, peripheral oedema or nocturnal hypoxaemia (KC adds secondary polycythaemia).
The patient **must have stopped smoking** because of the fire risk. KC confirms abstinence with carboxyhaemoglobin <3%.
Davidson: **at least 15 h/day at 2–4 L/min** to reach PaO2 >8 kPa; more benefit above 20 h/day.

blocks.text: **The books disagree on LTOT hours and flow.** Davidson says ≥15 h/day at 2–4 L/min; KC Essentials says 19 h/day at 1–3 L/min; Step-Up says ≥18 h/day. Quote Davidson's minimum of 15 h/day.
**FEV1/FVC cut-off for obstruction.** KC Essentials uses <75%; Davidson (and Zero to Finals) use **<0.7** post-bronchodilator. Use Davidson's 0.7.

cards.front: Chronic cough with normal examination, CXR and spirometry: three commonest causes?
cards.back: Cough-variant asthma, post-nasal drip (rhinitis/sinusitis) and GORD. Also check for an ACE inhibitor.

cards.front: What proportion of ACE-inhibitor users develop a dry chronic cough?
Low-pitched 'bovine' cough with hoarseness: mechanism and classic cause?
cards.back: Vocal cord palsy, typically from lung cancer invading the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Stops for breath after about 100 m or a few minutes on the flat.
Normal PaO2, low PaCO2, alkalosis. Exclude thromboembolism before making the diagnosis.
Partial obstruction of a major airway (larynx, trachea, main bronchus). Investigate urgently.

cards.front: Massive haemoptysis: threshold (K&C/KC) and the usual mechanism of death?
cards.back: >200 mL in 24 h; death is from asphyxiation, not blood loss.

cards.front: Which way do you position a patient with massive haemoptysis from a known side?
cards.back: Bleeding side down, to protect the good lung.

cards.front: Shoulder-tip pain in respiratory disease points to?
Davidson Box 17.8: roughly what share of clubbing is thoracic, and what share congenital/familial?
Clubbing in a COPD patient: what does it mean?
cards.back: Not part of uncomplicated COPD. Look for lung cancer, bronchiectasis or fibrosis.

cards.front: Horner's syndrome in a smoker with shoulder pain suggests?
Bronchial breathing + increased vocal resonance + whispering pectoriloquy = ?
Normal cricosternal distance in full expiration?
cards.back: 3–4 finger-breadths; reduced in hyperinflation from severe airflow limitation.

cards.front: Minimum effusion volume to do more than blunt the costophrenic angle on CXR?

cards.back: Partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. It reduces craving and withdrawal and about doubles quit rates.
Stopped smoking; PaO2 <7.3 kPa, or 7.3–8 kPa with pulmonary hypertension, oedema or nocturnal hypoxaemia; ≥15 h/day at 2–4 L/min.

cards.front: Smoking plus asbestos exposure: combined lung cancer risk?
cards.back: About 90 times that of unexposed non-smokers (synergistic).

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most likely cause of the cough from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman started a new antihypertensive 2 months ago after a diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy. She now has a persistent tickly dry cough. Examination, CXR and spirometry are normal.
items.explanation: A drug started for diabetic nephropathy and hypertension is almost certainly an ACE inhibitor. These cause a dry cough in 10–15% of users, more often women.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man has had a cough for 4 months, worse at night and after jogging. He never wheezes. Examination and CXR are normal.
items.explanation: Nocturnal and post-exercise cough with no other findings fits cough-variant asthma, where cough can be the only symptom.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man coughs up large amounts of foul yellow-green sputum every morning, especially when he rolls onto his side. He had severe measles pneumonia as a child. He has coarse crackles and finger clubbing.
items.explanation: Copious purulent sputum brought up by changes in posture, a childhood pneumonia and clubbing point to bronchiectasis.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most likely cause of the breathlessness from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: COPD exacerbation with type II respiratory failure

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman, 10 days after a hip replacement, collapses with sudden breathlessness. She is centrally cyanosed, BP 82/50 mmHg, with a raised JVP. The chest is clear on auscultation.
items.explanation: Shock, central cyanosis and a raised JVP with a clear chest after surgery are Davidson's discriminators for massive PE.

items.stem: A 69-year-old long-term smoker is drowsy and breathless. He has a coarse flapping tremor of the outstretched hands, warm peripheries and a bounding pulse. His chest is hyperinflated.
items.explanation: Flap, warm hands and a bounding pulse are signs of CO2 retention. In a hyperinflated smoker this means COPD with type II failure.

items.stem: A 22-year-old student breathes deeply and fast before an exam. She has tingling around the mouth and carpopedal spasm. She is pink, the heart and lungs are normal, and the ABG shows normal PaO2, very low PaCO2 and alkalosis.
items.explanation: Paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm, no cyanosis and a respiratory alkalosis with normal PaO2 suggest psychogenic hyperventilation, after PE has been excluded. Compare DKA, which causes deep breathing with an acidosis.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with known bronchiectasis coughs up about 300 mL of fresh blood over 12 hours. CT before this episode showed disease mainly in the left lower lobe. He is alert, SpO2 91% on air, HR 112/min.
questions.leadIn: Which is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Give regular codeine linctus to suppress the cough
Lie him left side down and give high-flow oxygen
Arrange urgent flexible bronchoscopy to locate the bleeding
Lie him flat on his back with legs raised
questions.explanation: In massive haemoptysis the danger is asphyxiation. Position the patient with the **bleeding side down** so blood does not flood the good lung, give high-flow oxygen and resuscitate. Embolisation or surgery follow.
whyNot: Cough suppressants may increase the risk of asphyxia by stopping clearance of blood.
Bronchoscopy during active bleeding usually just shows blood throughout the airways. It is done once bleeding settles.
Lying flat with legs raised does not protect the unaffected lung and makes breathing harder.
Anticoagulation would worsen bleeding. Coagulopathy should be reversed.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has fever, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and a small right pleural effusion. CXR shows no consolidation. She also mentions nausea and dark urine.
questions.leadIn: Which part of the examination is most important to add?
options: Neurological examination of the upper limbs
questions.explanation: Davidson stresses examining the **abdomen in every patient with pleuritic pain**. Subdiaphragmatic problems (cholangitis, liver abscess, cholecystitis, pancreatitis) mimic pneumonia with fever, pleuritic pain and a small right effusion. Dark urine hints at biliary disease.
whyNot: Fundoscopy does not help assess a subdiaphragmatic source.
Calf examination is relevant for PE, but fever, dark urine and nausea point below the diaphragm.
Breast examination does not explain the acute febrile presentation.
A neurological upper-limb exam is for Pancoast tumours, not this picture.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with long-standing COPD (FEV1 45% predicted) is noted at review to have new finger clubbing. He has lost 4 kg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: A recognised feature of advanced COPD needing no action
A sign of chronic CO2 retention
A sign that suggests a new disease such as lung cancer
questions.explanation: Clubbing is **not** a feature of uncomplicated COPD. With weight loss, it should prompt investigation for lung cancer (or bronchiectasis/fibrosis).
whyNot: COPD itself does not cause clubbing, so it cannot be dismissed.
CO2 retention gives flap, warm hands and bounding pulse, not clubbing.
Steroids cause bruising and thin skin, not clubbing.
Cor pulmonale gives a raised JVP and oedema, not clubbing.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old smoker has right shoulder and arm pain for 3 months. On examination the right pupil is small and the right eyelid droops.
questions.leadIn: Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Horner's syndrome (miosis, ptosis) with shoulder/arm pain in a smoker is the classic presentation of an apical **Pancoast tumour** involving the sympathetic chain and brachial plexus.
whyNot: SVC obstruction gives facial/arm swelling and distended chest veins, not Horner's.
Basal pneumonia does not involve the cervical sympathetic chain.
An effusion gives stony dullness, not Horner's.
Recurrent laryngeal palsy gives hoarseness and a bovine cough.

questions.leadIn: Match each set of signs below with the most likely underlying lesion from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Lobar collapse from a blocked major bronchus

items.stem: Right lower zone: reduced expansion, stony dull percussion, absent breath sounds and vocal resonance. Trachea deviated to the left.
items.explanation: Stony dullness with absent sounds and resonance and a shift away is a large effusion.

items.stem: Right mid-zone: dull percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance and whispering pectoriloquy. Trachea central.
items.explanation: Bronchial breathing with increased vocal resonance and no shift means consolidation with a patent bronchus.

items.stem: Left upper zone: reduced expansion, dull percussion, reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance. Trachea pulled to the left.
items.explanation: Dullness with volume loss pulling the trachea towards the lesion and _reduced_ sounds indicates collapse behind a blocked major bronchus (with a patent bronchus you would hear bronchial breathing).

items.stem: A ventilated trauma patient becomes hypotensive and tachycardic. Left chest hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds; trachea deviated to the right.
items.explanation: Hyper-resonance with absent sounds, tracheal shift away and haemodynamic compromise is tension pneumothorax. Decompress at once.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted with acute severe asthma. She cannot finish sentences, SpO2 is 90% on air and on auscultation the chest is almost silent.
questions.leadIn: What does the silent chest most likely indicate?
options: Airflow too low to generate wheeze
questions.explanation: In acute severe asthma a **silent chest** means so little air is moving that no wheeze is produced. It is a life-threatening feature.
whyNot: Improvement brings better air entry, not silence with distress.
An effusion is localised and stony dull, not a globally silent chest.
Vocal cord dysfunction gives inspiratory noise, not silence.
Consolidation gives localised bronchial breathing.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with COPD has PaO2 6.9 kPa on air on two stable readings 3 weeks apart. He still smokes 10 cigarettes a day.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step regarding oxygen?
options: Prescribe LTOT for at least 15 h/day now
Insist on smoking cessation before LTOT is prescribed
questions.explanation: His PaO2 meets the threshold, but LTOT requires that the patient **has stopped smoking**, because oxygen and cigarettes are a fire hazard. Cessation support comes first.
whyNot: Smoking is a contraindication; he does not yet qualify.
Ambulatory oxygen carries the same fire risk and is not the answer.
Nocturnal oxygen has the same contraindication.
Two stable readings 3 weeks apart already confirm hypoxaemia.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with mild COPD asks whether stopping smoking now is worthwhile, as she has 'already damaged her lungs'.
questions.leadIn: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Stopping restores FEV1 to the never-smoker level
Stopping slows the rate of FEV1 decline to that of a non-smoker
Stopping has no effect once COPD is diagnosed
Stopping only helps if done before age 40
Stopping doubles the rate of FEV1 recovery each year
questions.explanation: On the Fletcher–Peto curve, quitting **slows the decline back to the non-smoker rate**. There may be a small improvement, but the damage is not fully reversed. Stopping is the only intervention that changes the course of COPD.
whyNot: Quitting does not fully reverse the damage, so FEV1 does not return to the never-smoker curve.
Cessation benefits patients at any stage.
Benefit is seen even when stopping at 45 or 65.
FEV1 does not keep recovering year on year; the gain is a slower rate of decline.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most likely cause of the haemoptysis from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man who smokes 30 a day has noticed streaks of blood in his sputum on and off for 6 weeks. His cough has changed character.
items.explanation: Repeated small streaks of blood and a changing cough in a heavy smoker are highly suggestive of lung cancer.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man recently arrived from a high-prevalence country has 2 months of night sweats, weight loss and blood-tinged sputum. CXR shows right apical shadowing.
items.explanation: Fever, night sweats and weight loss with apical shadowing suggest tuberculosis.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has a 2-day history of high fever, rigors and right pleuritic pain, and coughs up rust-coloured sputum.
items.explanation: Rusty sputum with an acute febrile lobar illness is classic pneumococcal pneumonia.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man has haemoptysis, rising creatinine and red cell casts in the urine. Anti-GBM antibodies are positive.
items.explanation: A pulmonary-renal syndrome with anti-GBM antibodies is Goodpasture's syndrome. Pocket Medicine advises ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA and urinalysis in this setting.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with COPD complains that she becomes breathless when lying flat and sleeps on three pillows. She has no cardiac history; JVP is not raised and there is no oedema.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation of her orthopnoea?
options: It can occur in COPD because the diaphragm is pushed up when supine
It indicates a large pleural effusion
It is diagnostic of psychogenic breathlessness
questions.explanation: Orthopnoea is common in COPD as well as heart disease. Lying flat lets the abdominal contents push the diaphragm upwards and worsens airflow obstruction, so on its own it does not discriminate.
whyNot: Without cardiac history or signs, orthopnoea alone cannot prove LVF.
An effusion would give stony dullness, which is not described.
Psychogenic breathlessness rarely disturbs sleep and occurs at rest.
Nothing suggests diaphragmatic paralysis; COPD explains it.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man becomes breathless after walking about 100 m on level ground and has to stop. He manages to dress himself without difficulty.
questions.leadIn: What is his MRC dyspnoea grade?
questions.explanation: Stopping for breath after about 100 m on the flat is **MRC grade 4**. Grade 5 is breathlessness on dressing or being housebound.
whyNot: Grade 1 is breathlessness only on strenuous exercise.
Grade 2 is breathlessness hurrying or on a slight hill.
Grade 3 is walking slower than peers or stopping at own pace.
Grade 5 is too breathless to leave the house or dress.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old lifelong smoker has a hoarse voice and a weak, low-pitched cough that sounds 'like a cow'.
questions.leadIn: Which structure is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: A **bovine cough** with hoarseness reflects vocal cord paralysis, usually from lung cancer infiltrating the **left recurrent laryngeal nerve**.
whyNot: Phrenic palsy causes a raised hemidiaphragm, not hoarseness.
Sympathetic chain involvement causes Horner's syndrome.
SVC obstruction causes facial and arm swelling.
Bronchial obstruction causes collapse or monophonic wheeze, not hoarseness.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man is seen at a smoking-cessation clinic. He wants a drug that reduces craving by partially stimulating nicotinic receptors.
questions.leadIn: Which drug fits this description?
questions.explanation: **Varenicline** is an oral partial agonist at the α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. It eases withdrawal and craving and roughly doubles quit rates.
whyNot: KC Essentials notes that the mode of action of bupropion in smoking cessation is not clear; it is not a nicotinic partial agonist.
Nicotine replacement supplies nicotine itself; it is not the partial agonist described.
Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist used in alcohol/opioid dependence.
Disulfiram is used in alcohol dependence.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old non-smoking teacher has a dry cough for 5 months. She is not on any regular medication. Examination, CXR and spirometry are normal. She has frequent throat clearing and a feeling of something dripping at the back of her throat, with a blocked nose.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Step 1: chronic cough with normal examination, CXR and spirometry in a non-smoker not on an ACE inhibitor. Step 2: the three causes behind almost all such cases are cough-variant asthma, post-nasal drip and GORD. Step 3: nasal blockage, throat clearing and a dripping sensation point to **post-nasal drip** from rhinitis/sinusitis.
whyNot: Unlikely in a non-smoker with normal CXR, and nothing suggests it.
ILD gives fine crackles and usually progressive breathlessness.
Bronchiectasis produces copious purulent sputum, not a dry cough.
Pertussis can last up to 3 months but would not explain nasal drip symptoms at 5 months.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old ex-smoker has had a cough for 2 months. The trachea is deviated to the right; the right upper zone is dull with reduced expansion and reduced breath sounds. CXR shows a raised horizontal fissure and a right hilar mass.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Right upper lobe collapse from an obstructing tumour
questions.explanation: Step 1: dullness means solid or fluid. Step 2: the trachea moves **towards** the lesion, so there is volume loss (collapse or fibrosis), not fluid or air pushing. Step 3: _reduced_ breath sounds suggest a blocked central bronchus. Step 4: a raised fissure and hilar mass in an ex-smoker means **RUL collapse from an obstructing carcinoma**.
whyNot: Uncomplicated consolidation causes no mediastinal shift and gives bronchial breathing.
Pneumothorax is hyper-resonant, not dull.
A large effusion pushes the trachea away and is stony dull at the base.
Bronchiectasis gives coarse crackles and copious sputum, without a hilar mass.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has had haemoptysis twice this week. His CXR is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which statement best guides the next step?
options: A normal CXR excludes serious disease, so reassure
Arrange bronchoscopy and CT despite the normal CXR
Prescribe a cough suppressant and review in 6 months
questions.explanation: Step 1: haemoptysis is serious until proven otherwise. Step 2: a normal CXR does **not** exclude cancer, and Davidson recommends bronchoscopy once bleeding settles and CTPA if needed. Step 3: in fairness, Kumar notes that CT and bronchoscopy find a cause in only about 5% when the CXR is normal, but they are still done because the cause matters.
whyNot: A normal CXR does not exclude serious disease.
Empirical TB treatment without evidence is inappropriate.
Delay could miss a cancer; suppressants also mask symptoms.
Embolisation is reserved for massive, life-threatening bleeding.

questions.theme: Signs in the hands and face
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most likely explanation for the sign described, using the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with asthma has just had nebulised salbutamol. Her outstretched hands show a fine tremor; her pulse is 104/min.
items.explanation: A fine tremor and tachycardia after a β2-agonist are drug effects.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD on oral prednisolone for years has thin skin with extensive bruising on his forearms.
items.explanation: Bruising and thin skin are signs of chronic glucocorticoid use in the respiratory hand exam.

items.stem: A 64-year-old smoker has a swollen, plethoric face and distended veins over his upper chest wall.
items.explanation: Facial swelling and dilated chest wall veins indicate SVC obstruction, usually from a central lung tumour.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has progressive breathlessness for 2 years, a dry cough, finger clubbing and fine late inspiratory 'velcro' crackles at both bases.
items.explanation: Clubbing with bibasal fine crackles and progressive breathlessness fits IPF (clubbing in about two-thirds).

questions.theme: Health education and prevention in respiratory disease
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single most appropriate preventive measure from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Varenicline with a target stop date
Switching to a non-smoke cooking fuel
Asbestos exposure history and workplace advice

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman who smoked 30 pack-years and quit 5 years ago asks about checking for lung cancer. She has no symptoms.
items.explanation: Pocket Medicine: annual low-dose CT for ages 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years, current or quit within 15 years (about 20% fewer lung cancer deaths).

items.stem: A 35-year-old nurse, vaccinated with BCG at school, shares a household with her brother, who has just been diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary TB. She is well.
items.explanation: Close contacts of TB are screened with a CXR and a Mantoux test or an interferon-γ assay. She has already had BCG, so screening for infection is the step needed.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with moderate COPD has stopped smoking. He feels anxious, deconditioned and avoids walking because of breathlessness. PaO2 on air is 9.1 kPa.
items.explanation: Pulmonary rehabilitation (exercise, education, nutrition) improves symptoms, exercise tolerance and confidence. His PaO2 is too high for LTOT.

items.stem: A rural woman cooks daily over an indoor open wood fire in a poorly ventilated kitchen and has a chronic productive cough. She has never smoked.
items.explanation: Indoor biomass-fuel smoke is a major cause of respiratory disease in developing countries. Davidson advises non-smoke cooking devices or alternative fuels.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with COPD has a PaO2 of 7.8 kPa on air on two stable occasions 3 weeks apart. He stopped smoking 2 years ago. He has bilateral ankle oedema and echo shows pulmonary hypertension.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: No oxygen, as PaO2 is above 7.3 kPa
Long-term oxygen therapy for at least 15 hours a day
questions.explanation: PaO2 7.3–8 kPa **plus** pulmonary hypertension, oedema or nocturnal hypoxaemia qualifies for LTOT (Davidson: ≥15 h/day at 2–4 L/min, aiming for PaO2 >8 kPa), and he has stopped smoking.
whyNot: 7.3–8 kPa qualifies when pulmonary hypertension or oedema is present.
He meets the LTOT criteria; oxygen only during exacerbations falls far short of the 15 h/day Davidson specifies.
CPAP is not oxygen therapy and does not correct chronic hypoxaemia; he meets the LTOT criteria.
Short bursts before exertion do not provide the at least 15 h/day that LTOT requires.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman reports breathlessness with 'not being able to get a satisfying breath', frequent sighs and tingling fingers. She sleeps well and feels better playing tennis. Examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: Before diagnosing psychogenic hyperventilation, which condition must be excluded?
questions.explanation: Davidson warns that thromboembolism can present as unexplained breathlessness without other features and should **always** be considered before diagnosing psychogenic hyperventilation.
whyNot: Rhinitis causes nasal symptoms and cough, not this picture.
GORD causes heartburn and cough rather than dyspnoea with paraesthesiae.
Costochondritis causes localised tender chest pain.
Iron deficiency without anaemia does not cause hyperventilation.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the diagnosis that fits best, choosing from the options above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Kyphoscoliosis with type II respiratory failure

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman is woken most nights by chest tightness and wheeze. Her home peak flow varies widely from morning to evening. She had eczema as a child.
items.explanation: Nocturnal waking, diurnal variability on peak flow monitoring and atopy fit asthma.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with severe spinal deformity since childhood is increasingly breathless and has morning headaches and daytime sleepiness.
items.explanation: Morning headache in a breathless patient with chest wall disease signals CO2 retention, i.e. type II failure from kyphoscoliosis.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has become slowly more breathless over a year. He has had three episodes of pleuritic chest pain in different parts of his chest. CXR is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Recurrent pleuritic pain at different sites in a chronically breathless patient should raise suspicion of thromboembolic disease.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a non-productive cough is examined. Over the right lower zone there is reduced expansion, stony dull percussion and absent breath sounds and vocal resonance, with an area of bronchial breathing just above the dull zone. The trachea is central.
questions.leadIn: Which single diagnosis best accounts for all of these signs?
questions.explanation: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds and vocal resonance is a pleural effusion. Davidson's examination diagram also shows **bronchial breathing (or crackles) just above the effusion**, so that band does not mean a second lesion such as pneumonia.
whyNot: Consolidation is dull, not stony dull, and gives bronchial breathing with increased vocal resonance over the dull area itself.
Collapse is dull rather than stony dull and pulls the trachea towards the lesion; here it is central.
A pneumothorax is resonant or hyper-resonant, not stony dull.
Upper lobe fibrosis gives upper-zone signs and pulls the trachea towards it.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a chronic cough productive of sputum. He mentions his sputum is yellow most days, even though he has no fever. He has known asthma with eosinophilia.
questions.leadIn: What best explains the sputum colour?
questions.explanation: Yellow/green sputum is coloured by cells, either neutrophils **or eosinophils**. In asthma, eosinophils give the same appearance, so colour alone does not mean infection.
whyNot: Colour alone does not prove bacterial infection; no fever is present.
Carbon gives black specks in mucoid sputum.
Pulmonary oedema gives pink, frothy sputum.
Blood gives red or rusty sputum, not yellow.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with right-sided signs has a CXR showing only blunting of the right costophrenic angle.
questions.leadIn: Approximately what is the minimum effusion volume needed to do more than blunt the costophrenic angle on a CXR?
questions.explanation: Kumar: an effusion needs to exceed about **500 mL** before it does much more than blunt the costophrenic angle. Larger ones give a meniscus rising into the axilla.
whyNot: Far too small to be seen clearly on a PA film.
Still too small to go beyond blunting.
Below Kumar's 500 mL figure.
Volumes this large opacify much of the hemithorax and may shift the mediastinum.

ospe.identify: Finger clubbing: loss of the nail-fold angle, increased nail curvature, AP depth at nail base greater than at the DIP joint. Next: CXR; think lung cancer, bronchiectasis, fibrosis, empyema.
Clubbed finger next to a normal finger. Compare the nail-bed angle and bulbous distal phalanx; not a feature of uncomplicated COPD.
Left upper lobe collapse: opacified left upper/mid zone with volume loss; trachea and heart pulled to the left. Suspect an obstructing bronchial lesion.
Large pleural effusion: dense homogeneous opacity with a meniscus on an erect film; mediastinum shifted away if massive.
Normal PA chest X-ray: check view (PA vs AP), centring, trachea, right hemidiaphragm 2–3 cm higher, CTR <50%, mediastinum, hila, lung fields.

Pneumothorax: a visible visceral-pleura line with loss of lung markings beyond it. In a large pneumothorax the mediastinum shifts away and the diaphragm on that side is pushed down. A rim over 2 cm means at least 50% (large).
Bronchial artery angiogram: dilated right bronchial artery feeding massive haemoptysis in post-TB bronchiectasis, treated by embolisation.
